title: Does the Chain Loop Back?
statement:
A singly linked list has been laid out in an array. The nodes are numbered 0 … n − 1, and next[i] is the number of the node that comes after node i, or -1 if node i points to nothing. So next[i] is exactly node i's .next pointer, and -1 is null.

The head of the list is node 0. Start there and keep following next. Return true if you ever come back to a node you already visited (the list has a loop), and false if you reach -1.

Nodes that cannot be reached from node 0 do not belong to the list. Ignore them, even if they point at each other.

Aim for O(1) extra memory, and treat next like real pointers: a real linked list does not tell you its length, so do not rely on n to decide when to stop.

examples.why: 0 → 3 → 2 → 1 → 0. Node 1 points back at the head, so the walk never ends.
0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 1. The loop does not pass through the head, so "did I get back to node 0?" is the wrong test.
The list is just node 0. Nodes 1 and 2 point at each other, but they cannot be reached from the head.

hints: The easy way remembers every node you have visited. Can you detect a loop while remembering only a couple of positions?
Picture two runners on a track, one twice as fast as the other. On a straight road that ends, what happens? On a loop?
Move slow one step and fast two steps at a time. If fast hits -1, there is no loop. If they ever stand on the same node, there is.

explain.intuition:
Starting at the head and following pointers, there are only two possible shapes: a straight line that ends in null, or a line that runs into a loop and circles it forever (it looks like the letter ρ). A set of visited nodes tells them apart, but costs O(n) memory.

Floyd's trick uses two pointers instead. slow takes one step at a time, fast takes two. On a line, fast reaches the end first, and you are done. In a loop, once both are inside it, fast gains exactly one node on slow per step, so the gap shrinks by one every step and must hit zero: they meet. That happens within one lap of slow, so the walk is O(n) and the memory is two variables.

The array form is the same problem: p = next[p] is p = p.next, and -1 is null. The same two-runner code works on real nodes, which is why it does not use n.
steps: Loop while fast and the node after it both exist (are not -1).
If the loop ends because fast ran off the end, return false.
pitfalls: Checking slow === fast before moving. Both start at the head, so it is true immediately.
Only checking next[fast] and not fast itself (or the other way round). The fast pointer takes two steps, and either one can land on -1.
Testing "did the walk get back to node 0". The loop can start anywhere in the list, as in the second example.

solutions.title: Remember visited nodes
solutions.idea: Walk from the head and keep a set of nodes seen. Seeing one twice means a loop; reaching -1 means none.

solutions.title: Slow and fast pointers (Floyd)
solutions.idea: One pointer moves one step, the other two. On a dead-end list the fast one falls off; in a loop it catches the slow one from behind.

followups: Return the node where the loop starts. After the two pointers meet, what happens if you move one back to the head and walk both one step at a time?
Return the length of the loop using O(1) memory.
Here you know n, so "walk n steps and see if you are still going" also works in O(1) memory. Why does that not carry over to a real linked list?
